In the USA, if a copyright infringement case has been decided by the judicial system to be fair use, is it more accurate to say that a) copyright infringement occurred but it was legally excused, or b) copyright infringement did not occur?

message.content: The U.S. copyright system treats fair use differently than many people assume. Fair use is not a defense that excuses a violation which already happened. Rather, it defines the outer limits of what copyright law actually covers. A use deemed to be fair simply does not constitute infringement under any standard. This matters because calling it a "defense" implies the original act was unlawful and then forgiven, which is the wrong legal frame. The correct answer is (b).

The Supreme Court has characterized fair use as a limitation on the scope of copyright, not as a justification for infringement. In other words, fair use uses are outside the scope of the exclusive rights granted by copyright. So the answer is (b) — copyright infringement did not occur.
